comparator.name: Religious Studies
comparator.route: Cultural and Political Impact of Religion specialisation with 15-EC university/personal minor
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 regulations specify eight 7.5 EC units in each of the first two years. Year three has a 15 EC university or personal minor from another faculty, two of three faculty units, one of two specialisations, a thesis seminar, Science Communication and a 10 EC thesis. The ordinary minor and the two named faculty options are shown. The Cultural and Political Impact of Religion specialisation reflects the broad contemporary public-life emphasis of the degree. Quranic Arabic plus an optional module is an alternative to the minor. Other approved routes and substitutions have their own conditions.

routeSelection.route: Cultural and Political Impact of Religion specialisation with 15-EC university/personal minor
routeSelection.basis: Retain the existing Cultural and Political Impact of Religion specialisation for its documented contemporary social/political emphasis, without reference to UCR fit. Instantiating the ordinary university/personal minor at 15 EC preserves genuine choice; the first two faculty options satisfy the separate choose-two rule. Mutually exclusive and Board-approved alternatives are not stacked.

core: Religious narratives, visual cultures and philosophical meaning

candidates.label: Religion and environmental sustainability
candidates.rationale: General environmental study can address climate and sustainability but does not provide sustained study of religious responses to environmental change.

candidates.label: Religion, sexual health and spiritual care
candidates.rationale: General ethics, psychology and development offer related concepts but do not provide the religious frameworks and supervised care practice needed for this direction.

candidates.label: Religion education
candidates.rationale: Education and youth development can inform discussion of learning and radicalisation but do not provide sustained religion subject study and religion-specific teaching methods.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
trace: establishes how law, social institutions and justice interact, providing a foundation for studying religious freedom and religion in public life without claiming specialist religion law
studies human-rights law and its historical-philosophical foundations, including natural-law traditions, as a concrete basis for freedom of religion and speech questions
compares constitutional institutions, fundamental rights and remedies across jurisdictions, providing legal tools for questions of freedom and public authority
examines arguments about God, meaning, freedom and responsibility while teaching philosophical analysis; it supplies philosophical inquiry into belief rather than a full philosophy-of-religion course
develops moral reasoning through major ethical theories and applied problems, supporting the target's religion-and-ethics questions without being relabelled comparative religious ethics
compares accounts of self and consciousness, including Buddhist approaches, providing a specific cross-traditional philosophical contribution rather than a survey of Buddhism
provides concepts of authority, liberty, justice and political obligation needed to analyse religious claims and political order
uses legal, political, historical and social perspectives on conflict, identity and peacebuilding to contextualise religion-and-conflict questions
introduces sociological theory, institutions and race/gender/class analysis for examining belief communities and social identity; it is not presented as sociology of religion
teaches qualitative research design, interpretation and reflexivity for investigating lived meanings and communities without claiming religion-specific ethnography
studies civil society, solidarity, public spheres and migrant inclusion through theory and an organisation-based project, supporting religion, migration and public-life questions
examines how social contexts, groups and norms shape beliefs and behaviour, providing a psychological lens on identity without substituting for psychology of religion
studies youth radicalisation and educational prevention through protective factors, belonging and school climate; this supports the interest in extremism without presuming a religious cause
examines religious, social and gendered identities through ancient material culture across several world regions
studies how western-African visual forms embody religious and social meaning and addresses their museum and colonial histories
studies Renaissance art and architecture in exchange with Islamic courts and wider Mediterranean cultures, supplying a specific historical cross-cultural perspective
analyses how museums and curatorial strategies shape public interpretation of art, complementing religious visual-heritage questions without assuming religion-specific exhibits
directly examines how Athenian democracy was intertwined with myth and religion and expressed through art, literature and architecture

develops art-historical interpretation, visual analysis and academic writing for studying meaning and identity in religious images and heritage; the methods remain art-historical rather than religious-studies methods
traces themes of mortality, duty and community in epic, tragedy and confessional writing, developing textual interpretation relevant to narratives of belief
compares mythic narrative traditions including Indian, Greek, Byzantine and Arabic material and their transmission through text, image, orality and performance
studies storytelling, power, race and systemic exclusion through media production, supplying a specific identity-and-representation lens without treating race as religion
studies how religious and other social changes shape Western visual art and develops close visual analysis of paintings

alternatives.label: Religion, cultural heritage & political conflict
alternatives.concept: Study belief and its place in public life through myth, visual art, archaeology, and philosophy. Use law, politics, sociology, and psychology to investigate rights, identity, and conflict.
alternatives.labelReason: The composition follows belief, visual heritage and political life through myth, art and archaeology, philosophy, rights, sociology and conflict study.
progression: Foundations in law, philosophy, sociology and myth precede visual analysis, constitutional law, ethics and interpretation. Advanced courses bring together Athenian religion and politics, art-historical research, media and conflict. Current offerings and prerequisites pass.

selection.assessment: One coherent related-fields option has a clear strand in religious narratives, visual heritage and public life. Environmental sustainability, spiritual care and religion education lack sufficient integrated religious study in the current UCR courses. That academic limitation is separate from the timetable.

blocks: Religious narratives, philosophy and visual heritage
Both interpret narratives and their transmission. UCR studies myth in literature and other media; Groningen explicitly studies the use of religious texts.
Both interpret visual forms with religious meaning. UCR focuses on African visual and heritage traditions; Groningen studies religious images through iconography.
Both study how religion and politics shape one another. UCR concentrates on Athenian democracy, myth and ritual; Groningen also considers modern politics, conflict and peacebuilding.
Both develop philosophical analysis of belief and questions about God. UCR is a wider introduction to philosophy.
Both teach ethical reasoning. Groningen combines religion, ethics and care; UCR studies more general ethical theories and applications.
UCR qualitative methodology is useful for community inquiry, but it is not a sufficiently direct counterpart to the comparator's religion-specific research-design course.
The comparator has a dedicated religion-specific thesis-design seminar; no scheduled UCR course reproduces that formation.
The comparator requires a credited 10-EC independent thesis in Religious Studies. UCR optional independent research is shown in parallel but remains outside the scheduled 180 EC.
The comparator's science communication is explicitly about communicating religion research; no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart.
UCR contains religion-related cultural material but no sustained course in Christianity's history, sources and practice.
General humanities and social-science methods do not reproduce an introduction to the concepts and methods of Religious Studies.
The schedule has qualitative and social inquiry but no course in anthropology of religion.
World Myth & Literature and Philosophy of Mind include Indian or Buddhist material but do not provide a full course in South Asian religions.
No scheduled UCR course provides sustained study of Judaism's history, sources and practice.
General psychology and sociology courses support analysis of belief and identity but do not teach psychology and sociology of religion.
Mediterranean art history includes Islamic courts, but no scheduled UCR course provides sustained study of Islamic history, sources and practice.
No scheduled UCR course provides a sustained theory-and-practice study of religious ritual.
Media & Race supplies an identity-and-power lens, but it does not directly study religion, media and popular culture.
Sociology and social psychology address diversity and identity generally, but not new religious movements or lived religious diversity.
The comparator's genuine 15-EC university or approved personal minor remains visible without invented content.
General sustainability courses were not inserted merely to imitate a religion-and-climate option; the comparator's religious and spiritual framing remains unmatched.
UCR archaeology and environmental study do not reproduce the historical, sociological and spatial analysis of sacred space.
The complete UCR programme addresses selected cultural and political effects through related disciplines, but does not reproduce the comparator's religion-specific specialisation.

notes.text: Groningen offers sustained study of Christianity, Judaism, Islam, South Asian religions, ritual and methods for studying religion. UCR offers related perspectives on belief through literature, visual heritage, philosophy and social inquiry.

audience.programmeDescription: Religious Studies at the University of Groningen examines traditions, rituals, sacred texts and the role of religion in society. The degree includes a specialisation, a minor and a thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR option focuses on religious narratives, visual heritage and the place of belief in public life. Groningen offers more sustained study of religious traditions and specialist methods.
